historical_timeline.summary: Commanded VMF-214, the Black Sheep Squadron.
Shot down and captured; approximately 20 months of captivity followed.
Alcohol-related impairment followed a recurrent course with sober periods and relapses; PTSD is applied only retrospectively.

claims.statement: Gregory Boyington was born December 4, 1912, in Coeur d’Alene, Idaho.
Boyington commanded Marine Fighting Squadron 214 and received the Medal of Honor.
Boyington was shot down January 3, 1944, and spent approximately 20 months as a Japanese prisoner of war.
Marine Corps reporting describes Boyington as beaten, interrogated, and nearly starved during captivity.
A military scholarly review of a researched biography documents longstanding alcohol-related impairment, periods of sobriety, and later relapses.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports a historical alcohol-use problem but not uninterrupted eventual sobriety.

claims.statement: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a retrospective interpretation of Boyington’s combat and captivity history, not a documented lifetime diagnosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Keep the retrospective attribution distinct from the synthetic active diagnosis.

claims.statement: The roster’s phrase ‘eventual sobriety’ overstates a recurrent course that included both sustained sober periods and relapse.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record recovery and relapse together rather than forcing a single final-state narrative.

documentation.chief_complaint: Six-week alcohol use disorder and PTSD follow-up

hpi.narrative: Mr. Boyington returns six weeks after his intake visit, where he chose behavioral treatment for alcohol use disorder and was referred for trauma-focused psychotherapy. He began prolonged exposure therapy with Dr. Lee in behavioral health in early July and has attended five weekly sessions; Dr. Lee's consultation report came this morning. He has also gone to his veteran recovery peer group most weeks. Before treatment he drank most days, usually seven to nine drinks. In the six weeks since intake he drank on about four days, usually five beers. After a run of nightmares in the third week of therapy, when the imaginal exposure work began, he had one day of more than six drinks. He did not drive and called a peer from his group the next morning. He has had no tremor, sweats, or withdrawal symptoms. He sleeps about five and a half hours, with nightmares about twice a week instead of most nights, and he startles less at loud noises. He has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm since intake and still keeps the written safety plan in his wallet. He has lost 1.3 kg and attributes it to fewer drinks.

documentation.chief_complaint: Low back pain for two days after lifting

hpi.narrative: Mr. Boyington asked for a same-day visit for low back pain. Two days ago, while helping a friend move, he lifted a heavy box with his back bent and felt a sudden pull across the left lower back. The pain is a dull ache with sharp catches when he bends, twists, or gets out of a chair, and it is easing a little each day. It does not travel into the legs. He has no numbness, tingling, or weakness, and no change in bladder or bowel control or numbness between the legs. He has had no fever, weight loss beyond the expected loss since he cut down on drinking, or prior back injury. Ice and walking help. The pain woke him on both nights, and on the second night he had a nightmare for the first time in about two weeks. He felt an urge to have a drink to get back to sleep, did not, and called a peer from his recovery group instead. He has not drunk alcohol since his review last week. He has taken two doses of ibuprofen 400 mg. A friend offered him leftover muscle relaxant tablets, which he declined and asked about today.

referral.question: Co-occurring alcohol use disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in a 44-year-old veteran. Please confirm the PTSD diagnosis, provide trauma-focused psychotherapy alongside his alcohol treatment, and share your assessment of risk
referral.pertinent_history: Combat service and prolonged captivity as a prisoner of war, with nightmares, startle, avoidance, and broken sleep; he drinks at night to get to sleep. Drinks most days, usually seven to nine drinks; AUDIT-C 10, PCL-5 39, PHQ-9 9 with item 9 scored 0. No withdrawal history. Today's structured safety assessment found no current suicidal ideation, intent, or plan; access to lethal means was reviewed and a collaborative safety plan written. He chose behavioral treatment for alcohol use disorder over medication for now and takes no medicines. Supports include family, veteran peers, and a recovery peer group
questions: Does he meet criteria for PTSD, and is a PCL-5 of 39 a reasonable baseline for measuring progress?
Which trauma-focused psychotherapy do you recommend, and can it start while he is still drinking?
How should his alcohol treatment be coordinated with trauma therapy, and is there a point at which you would advise adding medication?
Please reassess suicide risk and help keep his safety plan current
What do you advise for his sleep and nightmares?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Boyington was referred by Dr. Marquez for evaluation and trauma-focused psychotherapy. At the first session in early July a structured diagnostic interview confirmed post-traumatic stress disorder related to combat and captivity, with intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of reminders, hypervigilance, and startle. He chose prolonged exposure therapy and has attended five weekly sessions. The run of nightmares that followed the start of imaginal exposure in the third week was followed by one day of heavy drinking; he used his relapse plan and returned to the next session. He now drinks on about four days in six weeks, has fewer nightmares, and startles less. He reports no suicidal thoughts since intake and keeps his safety plan with him
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Marquez's referral and intake safety assessment, and today's AUDIT-C, PCL-5, and PHQ-9 alongside the intake scores

exam.finding: Well groomed, calm, good eye contact; no tremor or signs of intoxication
Normal rate, volume, and rhythm
Mood “better, still on edge”; affect mildly anxious, congruent, and reactive
Linear and goal-directed
No suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan; trauma-related intrusive memories without psychotic content
No hallucinations
Alert and fully oriented; attention and memory intact on interview
Good; links drinking to nightmares and uses his relapse plan

assessment.assessment: Diagnosis confirmed. The intake PCL-5 of 39 is a valid baseline. Today's 31 is an 8-point fall, short of the 10 points usually taken as meaningful change, but the course is early and nightmares and startle are improving

Drinking has fallen from most days to about four days in six weeks (AUDIT-C 10 to 5). The single heavy-drinking day followed the expected rise in distress early in exposure work, not disengagement. Concurrent treatment of both disorders is appropriate and does not need to wait for abstinence

Low acute risk: no current ideation, intent, plan, or preparatory behavior, and PHQ-9 item 9 is 0. Chronic risk factors are male sex, veteran status, alcohol use disorder, and PTSD; protective factors are engagement in treatment, veteran and recovery peers, family support, and a strong sense of service. The safety plan was reviewed with him today and remains current
Nightmares are part of the PTSD and are already easing with exposure therapy and less drinking

recommendations: Continue weekly prolonged exposure; I expect about four more sessions to complete the course
Continue behavioral alcohol treatment and the veteran recovery peer group. Revisit naltrexone or acamprosate with Dr. Marquez if heavy-drinking days recur during the rest of therapy
Avoid benzodiazepines and sedative sleep medicines, which can undermine exposure therapy and add to the risk with alcohol
Plan for nights after hard sessions: a call to a peer, no alcohol in the house, and the wind-down routine from therapy
Repeat PCL-5, AUDIT-C, and PHQ-9 at twelve weeks
For sleep, keep a regular rise time and do not use alcohol as a sleep aid; if insomnia persists after the course, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia
Keep the safety plan current, with the crisis line (988, press 1) in his phone
consultant_note.communication: Report sent to Dr. Marquez and discussed with her the same day; he agrees with the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Weekly prolonged exposure through the end of the course, then a booster session on request. Behavioral health will see him sooner for a rise in PCL-5, a return to heavy drinking, or any suicidal thoughts
